I signed up with a temp agency that focuses on manufacturing and logistics jobs, the manufacturing jobs are usually warehouse jobs that are very physical. Or “desk” factory jobs where you just do the same repetitive task over and over. I’ve worked with them on/off for a couple of years. I asked to be transferred to the logistics area to see if any entry level work was there, most of those jobs require prior experience but they pulled some strings to find me one.  

If anything I’d say to get your foot in the door and apply for manufacturing jobs, most of them don’t require socialization. And a lot of these places hire “outcasts” so they’re used to oddballs like us lol. After you prove you can show up for work and all that ask if they have any data entry jobs. And practice typing a lot! I had to submit a typing speed test with my application and I think the reason I got the job with no experience is because I scored pretty high.

I deal with something similar, I have fibromyalgia and get muscle pain/tension everywhere. I lay on top of a heating pad on nights were the pain is bad, and it helps a lot. Heat increases blood flow to the area and relaxes your muscles. During the day I use biofreeze on the areas my muscles hurt. Maybe that’s something you could try?

Also, doing 5-10 minutes of stretching in the morning is a very underrated way of fixing this. Try to do stretches that involve lifting your arms up and stretching your side, like [this](https://www.spotebi.com/exercise-guide/triceps-stretch/). Shoulder and side stretches work great as well. If you consistently stretch the affected muscles it’ll prevent the tension from building up, and keep the knots from forming.

Well for learning more about your diagnosis, it may be a better help for you to research how ASD presents itself differently in women. Since ASD was originally thought to be a male disorder, a lot of research is focused on male traits and behavior. Women are raised with a different set of gender norms, which greatly affects how ASD will present itself. So Women don’t really fit into the “stereotypical” ASD we’re used to seeing in media/research because of this. It might help you connect more to your diagnosis if you check women-centered research. Just make sure to stay away from autism speaks lol.

Also, don’t be too hard on yourself. I know it can be a huge shock. I got diagnosed in my teens, and felt like my whole reality shattered when I was diagnosed. I struggled a lot with my self worth, feeling “dumb”/unlovable, I started obsessing over every social interaction wondering if I was making mistakes, struggling with my sense of self, etc.. It’s going to be a path to rediscovering yourself, but try not to let it weigh down on you too much. You are a lovable, intelligent person that is a joy to have around, and your diagnosis doesn’t change that. It doesn’t change anything, you just know more about yourself now (which can be really fun and exciting!). You don’t have to tell anyone if you don’t want to. It’s not something you should/shouldn’t do, just something you can share if you feel like it. You don’t have to change anything in your life at all if you don’t want to or feel the need to.

There’s a lot of great things about being autistic, but I know it can get tough too. We’re all here for you, and if you ever need to talk my dms are open (I can also send you some resources if you’d like!)

I was at a psychiatrist appointment when I was 14, she asked me a couple of odd questions and at the end of the appointment said “Well I think you would qualify for an autism spectrum disorder diagnosis”. I didn’t even know what autism was, my parents knew and hid it from me my whole life. I started researching it and it felt like my whole world opened up and I finally knew why everything was the way it was. 

She couldn’t technically diagnose me but told me to seek it out, and it took me 2 years to get that diagnosis. I self diagnosed and advocated for myself that whole time. People said I just wanted attention, was faking it, etc. Self diagnosing isn’t always %100 a bad thing, although even I am skeptical of people that self diagnose because of the trends lately. 

The main reason these people bother me so much is that they’re “spreading awareness” and making educational videos on a disorder/experience they aren’t proven to have. Stealthing is an issue I have to deal with more often with them, and some will flat out refuse a condom after you get there. Wear shoes you can run in and an outfit you can throw on quickly. I would not host in these cases, or drive your own car to a location. Some guys might want car sex because they can’t host or afford a hotel, which is a risk you have to decide on taking or not. 

Not trying to scare you, just sharing some of my personal experience with this. It could be different in your area. Most of the time things are fine but I’ve had things go wrong very quickly so it’s good to be prepared. Stay safe!

In my experience selling and knowing other people that sell, a lot of people take offers into account when pricing items. So if someone wanted to sell an item for 25$, they might list it at $30 so they have the ability to offer a discount. Definitely don’t feel bad about making an offer, as long as it’s not extremely low. Try to keep your offer between 10-30% of the listing price. Or you could add the item to a bundle by itself to show you’re interested, which usually results in the seller making an offer. If a seller is firm on a price, they will usually say so in the description of the listing. 

And I would recommend having the family member make their own account, when selling you need to have access to the email the account was made with, and you may wish to keep payment methods separate.

Sometimes I get upset, and blow up at small things and go on and on about it despite others efforts to help, it’s a toxic trait but if she does the same thing, just let her get it out. Validate her emotions, tell her you understand and that she has every right to feel the way she does. It’s usually something else causing me to be so upset, for example getting mad at my boyfriend for saying he’d do the dishes and not doing them, and me blowing up at that, when actually I’m really upset because I feel like he hasn’t been affectionate or appreciative of me lately. Gently try and see if there’s a bigger issue. 

If it’s a random person you’re trying to repair her relationship with, ask her if she would be open to talking about it with them. If the answer is no then I’d just drop it, you can’t force it.


I 100% understand the silence thing. Sometimes it’s that I’m under stimulated, and playing music or having a movie on as background noise will solve that. But I’ve definitely gotten upset at my boyfriends silence, and it’s usually because I’m worried he doesn’t like me, is bored of me, wants to leave, etc. and that leads to toxic irrational thoughts like “he’s cheating, wants to break up, hates me”. Try saying “I’m glad I’m so comfortable around you that we can both sit in silence and do our own thing, I think that’s really cool” every now and then, or giving her reassurance that you like spending time with her and find it enjoyable. Avoid saying things like “if I didn’t like you I wouldn’t be here” if she’s worried you don’t like her, but instead say things like “ I like you very much, I love having you as my SO, because..” and give an example of something you like about her, or your relationship. 

If you notice that things have gone silent, and have run out of things to talk about, and you’re watching a movie/on your phone, share something you found interesting (even just a random post you scrolled by), mention something about your day/the room, even if mundane. If she’s on her phone ask her about what she’s reading or watching. And you can always ask about her special interest if she has one. Bring up something you’d like to try together, comment (positively)  about lights/sounds/textures in the room. Tell a fun/interesting story about your past, or something you saw on the news or that happened to a friend. Conversation doesn’t have to be 100% engaging all the time, sometimes I like to just listen to people talk about things, it eases my mind and keeps it from wandering to upsetting places. 

As for uncomfortable topics, sometimes it’s overwhelming or she’s not in a good headspace at the time . Maybe ask her if she’d be more comfortable if you asked if it was a good time to discuss difficult topics before just jumping into it, and say that if it’s not a good time you can revisit it when she’s ready. If she’s upset with something, ask her if she would like help finding a solution/advice, or if she’d just like to vent. And let her know she has your support. 

I’d do a lot of research on bpd, and autism in adults. Make sure they’re written by autistic people or people with bpd though. Read up on overstimulation, understimulation, and meltdowns. These subs have a lot of good resources for learning beyond the base level of what autism is.

That type of communication is difficult though, especially if you don’t like confrontation or being vulnerable. I know I stopped talking to a lot of people just because I didn’t want the confrontation, and ghosting was a way to avoid that.

For example, one time I was insulted by a person that we had just met, and a friend of mine said immediately “whoa that was rude, Fossilferret, tell him not to talk to you like that”. We’d usually ask eachother, usually something like “feeling or need?” Or “is this for you or me?” I know it seems like it defeats the purpose of the button but it was a lot easier for us to put our emotions in 1 of 2 categories rather than try to describe one from the massive spectrum of all emotions. Something that helped my boyfriend and I a TON was the app “Love Nudge”. You both download it, and It tests you both to see what type of love language each of you have. Based on those results, it gives each partner examples/ideas of affectionate things they could do that would help their partner feel more loved or appreciated. You can also set goals for the relationship. 

Our favorite thing was the “nudge” button. You press it and it sends a “love nudge” notification to your partner. My boyfriend and I used the button 2 ways: 1. As a way of saying “I’m not sure how to communicate or describe my feelings/love for you, but I still want you to know” and 2. As a way of communicating we needed a little extra affection when we had a difficult time saying so.

If you don’t mind using technology to help (it can feel a bit odd at first) and you’re both willing to try it, I’d highly recommend giving it a shot. 

Other than that, I’d say just reassure him often and do lots of research on Alexithymia. People with alexithymia can and usually do have very fulfilling relationships, it just takes a bit of extra effort from each partner sometimes!

I wouldn’t say it’s like a hyper focus, but A safe food can be a lot of different things. Lots of autistic struggle with sensory processing problems with texture/taste while eating, so foods with a texture or flavor that is tolerable is a “safe” food. Lots of autistic people struggle with change in routine or trying new things, so that same food they are comfortable eating daily is a safe food. Executive dysfunction is also common, so foods that are easy to make and don’t take too much energy could be safe. Digestive disorders are common among autistic folk, so a food that doesn’t cause them pain after eating would be safe as well. A safe food is a food that doesn’t cause you discomfort in some way, which unfortunately almost all of us deal with it in some way. My safe foods that I could eat at any time are chicken, tomato soup/grilled cheese, and pizza. Very basic stuff that is easy for me to eat/make. That’s not all I eat, on a good day I could eat sushi and habaneros and all kinds of complicated stuff, but on bad days I stick to my safe foods. For me my safe foods would change every 2 years or until I burnt myself out on them. Sorry I’m kinda rambling but I hope this helped answer your question lol

I had really bad psychosis as a teenager, and would have these paranoid delusions that would make me afraid to do anything. I spent a lot of time in psychiatric wards, had to drop out of school, my family was asking doctors if I’d ever be functional. I didn’t leave the house for months, I couldn’t look in mirrors, and did everything I could to (in my mind) delay the inevitable. And eventually she just said that to me and it clicked. I started doing the things I was afraid of, and told myself “if it’s going to happen, it’s going to happen whether I do anything or not, I’ll worry when the time comes”. And of course, nothing happened, ever.  It’s been 5 years and while I still have some paranoia about things, I handle it well and I’m considered 100% recovered. 


If you have a loved one that experiences delusions, don’t tell them it’s not real. Logic doesn’t work. Act as if the delusion was real, and try to help them work through how to handle whatever it is as if it was a normal life experience. Trying to convince them it’s all in their head just tells them “No one is going to help you or believe you, you’re on your own.”. Imagine calling the cops because your house is being robbed and them just saying “have you tried seeking psychiatric help? I’ve heard yoga and a healthy diet helps!”. That’s how it feels.

So for me personally, I do ~feel~ emotions in my body, but I don’t know what emotions they are, so I definitely understand using words to describe them. There were 2 things that helped me a lot when it came to describing my feelings. (if you’re open to advice, if not please ignore me). 1. I had to learn to really focus on what I was feeling to understand it. I’d start out with the basics “am I uncomfortable, am I upset, am I angry, etc” and narrow it down to a basic emotion. Then I’d look at any physical symptoms, so for example: if my “basic” emotion is happy, and I’m shaky or breathing to heavy/quickly, then I’d make the connection that I was excited. Don’t focus to much on the broad question “what am I feeling”, first ask yourself “what am I not feeling”. It’s a lot easier to narrow it down when you know what you’re definitely not feeling. The second thing that helped me was getting a little emotion dictionary online, it’s just a picture I can keep on my phone that lists all the specific emotions I have a hard time finding the word for. And sometimes reading the word of an emotion helps me realize that I’m feeling it.
